titre: The 1883 Paris Convention, a Time Window Rather Than an Automatic Right
accroche: On March 20, 1883, eleven countries give an inventor six months to file elsewhere. Three years later, another treaty chooses the opposite, for books.
contenu_vulgarise:
On March 20, 1883, in a hall in Paris, delegates from eleven countries sign a text whose problem fits in a single sentence: a patent filed in Brussels in the morning protects nothing in Berlin in the afternoon. Each state decides alone who has the right to exploit an invention on its soil, and none recognizes the patent granted by its neighbor. An inventor who wants protection everywhere must therefore file everywhere, on the same day if possible, before a competitor reads the application in one country and refiles it elsewhere in his own name.

## A time window, not an automatic right

The Convention for the Protection of Industrial Property solves this problem without claiming to create a worldwide patent, something it never will. It sets up two mechanisms. The first is national treatment: a foreigner who files in a member country receives exactly the protection that country grants its own nationals, no more, no less. The second is the right of priority: whoever has filed an application in one member country has six months, for a patent, or three months, for an industrial design or model or a trademark, to file the same application elsewhere while keeping the date of the first filing as the reference. During that period, no one can set an intervening filing against them, or even the publication or working of the invention in the meantime. In the current text, these periods are twelve months for a patent and six months for a trademark or an industrial design.

Eleven countries sign the text on March 20, 1883: Belgium, Brazil, France, Guatemala, Italy, the Netherlands, Portugal, El Salvador, Serbia, Spain and Switzerland. It will be revised six times in less than a century, in Brussels in 1900, in Washington in 1911, in The Hague in 1925, in London in 1934, in Lisbon in 1958 and in Stockholm in 1967, without ever abandoning these two founding mechanisms.

## Three years later, another treaty, another logic

In 1886, ten countries sign, in Bern, a few hundred kilometers from Paris, a second treaty, the Berne Convention, to protect literary and artistic works. The two texts resemble each other in ambition, but not in mechanics: Berne forbids any formality, a book is protected as soon as it exists, in all member countries at once, with no filing and no deadline to meet. The Paris Convention, for its part, protects nothing automatically: each country keeps examining, granting or refusing a patent under its own rules, independently of what the others decide.

This difference is not an oversight by the drafters of 1883, it comes from the very nature of what they protect. A copyright is born of a gesture of creation that no one needs to verify; a patent requires an examination, an administrative decision, a risk of refusal, specific to each country. You cannot harmonize a right that exists only after an office's decision: you can only give its holder the time to run the same race elsewhere without losing the benefit. That time, six months or three, is what the Paris Convention invents in 1883, and what the Berne Convention, three years later, will never need.

repere.texte: In the 1883 text, the priority period of the Paris Convention is six months for a patent of invention, and three months for an industrial design or model and for a trademark; it is now twelve months for a patent or a utility model, and six months for a trademark or an industrial design.
repere.source: Paris Convention for the Protection of Industrial Property, March 20, 1883, Article 4; Stockholm text (1967), Article 4 C(1)

carte.punch: In 1883, a patent filed in Paris could wait six months before being refiled elsewhere.
carte.idee: On March 20, 1883, eleven countries agree on a time window: six months for a patent, three for a trademark, during which a first filing remains protected wherever it is refiled. Three years later, the Berne Convention will choose the opposite for books: no time window, because no formality.

quiz.question: Why does the 1883 Paris Convention give the inventor a priority period, rather than making the patent automatically valid in all member countries?
choix: Because the signatory countries did not yet have an administration able to examine foreign applications
Because the convention imposes a single patent common to all member countries, to be issued within the year
Because each country keeps examining and granting the patent under its own rules, independently of decisions made elsewhere
Because filing fees must be paid in each country before the period starts to run
quiz.explication: The convention does not create a worldwide patent: each country keeps its own independent decision. The priority period merely leaves time to file elsewhere without losing the benefit of the first filing date.

quiz_supplementaire.question: How many countries sign the Paris Convention on March 20, 1883?
quiz_supplementaire.explication: Eleven countries sign the text on March 20, 1883: Belgium, Brazil, France, Guatemala, Italy, the Netherlands, Portugal, El Salvador, Serbia, Spain and Switzerland.

quiz_supplementaire.question: In its 1883 text, what period does the Paris Convention allow for filing a trademark in another member country while keeping the date of the first filing?
quiz_supplementaire.explication: The 1883 text sets the priority period at three months for a trademark or an industrial design or model, and double that, six months, for a patent of invention.

quiz_supplementaire.question: Why could the Paris Convention not exempt patents from every formality, as the Berne Convention would do for books three years later?
choix: Because patents had no commercial value comparable to that of books in 1883
Because the signatory countries of 1883 did not yet have a ministry in charge of patents
Because the Berne Convention was discussed before the Paris one
Because a patent exists only after an administrative decision specific to each country, which no treaty can make automatic
quiz_supplementaire.explication: A copyright is born of a gesture of creation that no examination validates; a patent requires an administrative decision specific to each country, which no convention could standardize in 1883.
